rationale: The abstract and intro present a toy ReLU model in which polysemanticity is fully explained by sparse features stored in superposition, with phase changes and polytope geometry. The intro notes that clean neurons seem rare in LLMs, but the paper tests no LLM neurons, so it shows superposition is a plausible mechanism rather than the primary explanation in LLMs.

Scherlis et al. treat superposition as 'one form [of polysemanticity] that seems particularly fundamental' (Intro). Their toy capacity-allocation analysis finds that less important features become polysemantic when features outnumber neurons, more so with sparse or high-kurtosis inputs. The results are toy-only and the authors say polysemanticity can arise in multiple ways, so support for the LLM claim is weak.

In toy models, adding neurons per layer raises monosemanticity, which fits a capacity/superposition account. However, the abstract also finds that models can become more monosemantic at the same loss just by landing in a different local minimum (one with negative biases), so the polysemanticity is not forced by compression. Toy-only, mixed implications.

Sparse probing on 7 real LLMs (70M-6.9B) finds early-layer neurons in superposition: compound-word/n-gram features are represented by sparse combinations of massively polysemantic neurons (Fig. 2, 'Superposition in the Wild'), with weight-norm and negative-bias fingerprints. Middle layers show seemingly dedicated neurons, and the evidence is case-study and correlational, so it supports superposition as a major explanation without establishing it as primary.

The paper starts from superposition as the hypothesised cause of polysemanticity (Abstract). Overcomplete SAEs trained on Pythia activations find features that score as more interpretable than neurons or PCA/ICA directions, and they localise IOI behaviour more finely. This is indirect support: interpretability gains fit superposition but do not rule out other causes, and auto-interp metrics are the main evidence.

Decomposing a one-layer transformer's 512-neuron MLP into up to 131k SAE features turns polysemantic neurons (e.g. A/neurons/489, a mix of languages) into interpretable features. The authors cite interference weights and other observations 'you would expect from superposition' (Theories of Superposition). They also report that 'individual neurons can be polysemantic even in the absence of superposition' when activations are forced sparse, and that real superposition is denser and more structured than in toy models. The model is a small one-layer transformer, so support for the LLM claim is qualified.

Proposes 'incidental polysemanticity': theory and experiments show neurons become polysemantic even with ample neurons for all features, driven by random initialization plus regularization or neural noise (Abstract). This directly challenges the necessity-from-compression story, though the authors call it non-mutually exclusive and the experiments are in small or toy settings, not LLM neurons.

Studies universality of GPT-2 neurons across seeds (1-5% universal, usually interpretable). Polysemanticity is taken as known background, and superposition is discussed only in passing, e.g. redundant neurons being 'polysemantic with different sets of rarer features' (Sec. 6). The paper does not test the cause of polysemanticity.

Finds irreducible multi-dimensional (circular) features in GPT-2, Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and proposes a 'Multi-Dimensional Superposition Hypothesis' (Sec. 3). This revises what the superposed features look like rather than whether superposition explains neuron polysemanticity, so it is mostly orthogonal to the question.

Gives purely theoretical constructions showing networks can compute (e.g. pairwise ANDs, sparse boolean circuits) efficiently in superposition with far fewer neurons than features (Fig. 1, Sec. 3). This makes superposition more plausible as a strategy, but no LLM neurons are examined and the cause of observed polysemanticity is not tested.

Shows SAE latents on LLMs suffer feature absorption under hierarchical features because of the sparsity objective. This is a critique of the SAE tool, not evidence about why LLM neurons are polysemantic.

SAEs trained on randomly initialized Pythia transformers give auto-interp and reconstruction scores similar to trained models (Abstract). This weakens SAE interpretability as evidence that trained LLMs learned compressed superposed features, and the authors suggest the data itself may carry superposition that random networks preserve or amplify (Sec. 1, Sec. 4). It is methodological, does not directly test the cause of polysemanticity, and separates superposition from neuron polysemanticity (Related Work).

SAE stitching and meta-SAEs show SAE latents are neither complete nor atomic. This questions SAEs as finders of canonical units but does not address whether superposition explains neuron polysemanticity.
SAE probes do not beat baselines on LLM probing tasks (Fig. 1). This tests the downstream usefulness of SAEs and says nothing direct about the origin of polysemanticity.

Argues from token-representation norms and squared overlaps scaling as about 1/m that open LLMs operate in a 'strong superposition regime' (Sec. 4, around line 502-526), and links this to scaling laws. This supports superposition existing in LLMs, but the analysis covers embedding/unembedding representations rather than neurons and never addresses polysemanticity directly.

Across nine transformers (110M-70B), a 2x2 factorial design shows that sharing a word form produces more neuron overlap than sharing a meaning. The conclusion says 'a substantial portion of what current metrics call polysemanticity is lexical identity, not superposition' (Fig. 1: 'only a small remainder is genuine superposition'). The authors explicitly do not deny superposition, and the 57% confound ratio applies only to polysemous inputs (Limitations), so the result argues against 'primarily' without refuting superposition.
